briefing.headline: The simulation predicts leavers over the next 12 months would roughly halve, from 797 to 403 out of 5,000. Read this as a strong positive signal, not a forecast, especially since the 12-month window runs past the six-month trial.
briefing.most_at_risk: Long commuters (-55% leaving) and caregivers (-54%) gain the most because they get back travel time and family time, while managers, operations and finance carry the most risk because they expect to be the ones squeezing the same output into fewer hours around fixed deadlines like month-end close and audits.
risks: Nearly every voice welcomes the extra day but worries about cramming the same work into four days, so if workloads don't actually change the goodwill could turn into burnout and resentment.

The retention gain assumes the benefit lasts, so scrapping or scaling back after six months could leave morale and attrition worse than today, especially among the long commuters and caregivers who value it most.

Deadline-driven and coordinating roles (finance, operations, managers) may quietly absorb the extra pressure or work on their day off, which would hollow out the benefit for exactly the people who have to make it work.
design_changes: Agree concrete output measures with each team before launch, and say plainly what work will stop or shrink, such as cutting standing meetings, rather than relying on people simply working harder.
Publish the end-of-trial decision criteria and process upfront, and commit to a gradual adjustment rather than an abrupt return to five days if results are mixed.

Give deadline-heavy functions flexibility, such as staggered days off, rotas for client cover, or shifting the day around month-end, and give managers specific support and authority to re-plan workloads.
briefing.confidence: low, because the effect is almost identical across every group (-47% to -55%) and the sample voices are strikingly similar, which suggests the model isn't distinguishing between groups well; the voices also come mostly from office-based roles, and the numbers don't show what happens to leaving if the trial ends at six months.
